--- title: "Decomposition methods across trade and demography" subtitle: "A reproducible demonstration with the ddec R package" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("analysis/_setup.R") ``` ::: ## Motivation Trade economists decompose a country's gross exports into domestic value added, foreign value added and double counting [@hummels2001; @koopman2014; @wang2013; @borin2019]. Demographers decompose a difference in crude rates, life expectancy or population growth into contributions by age, factor or vital rate [@kitagawa1955; @dasgupta1993; @arriaga1984; @caswell1989]. The two literatures seldom cite each other, even though their methods share the same machinery: 1. Both partition an aggregate into **additive contributions** from structured factors. 2. The **Leontief inverse** $(I - A)^{-1}$ is the same mathematical object as the **fundamental matrix** $N = (I - U)^{-1}$ of an absorbing Markov chain [@kemeny1960; @caswell2001], which underlies multistate life tables and matrix population models. 3. The **non-uniqueness** of multi-factor decompositions is solved the same way in both fields, by averaging over all orderings (the Shapley value). This is what Das Gupta standardisation does in demography and what structural decomposition analysis does in input-output economics [@dietzenbacher1998; @shorrocks2013]. 4. The **LTRE** (sensitivity × parameter change) and **Leontief-based attribution** both decompose a scalar output of a matrix model into per-cell contributions, and their sensitivities have the same outer-product form. ## Pages * [GVC results](01-gvc-decomposition.qmd): Leontief, KWW, WWZ and Borin-Mancini on the same table. Every method's components sum to gross exports. * [Demographic results](02-demographic-decomposition.qmd): Kitagawa, Das Gupta, Arriaga and LTRE, with cross-checks against `DasGuptR`, `LEdecomp` and `popbio`. * [Structural parallels](03-structural-parallels.qmd): the matrix-inverse isomorphism, Shapley on both sides (including the order dependence of sequential decompositions), sensitivity-based attribution against the exact answer, the concept map, and the limits of the analogy. ## Data | Dataset | Content | Source | Real? | |---|---|---|---| | `leather` | 3 countries × 3 industries ICIO table | inherited from `icio`/`decompr` | toy example | | `icio_synth` | two 3 × 2 ICIO tables, "2010" and "2020" | `simulate_icio()`, `data-raw/get_icio_data.R` | **synthetic** | | `dk_mortality` | Danish deaths, population and $m_x$ by single age, 2000 and 2019 | Eurostat `demo_magec`, `demo_pjan`; `data-raw/get_demo_data.R` | real | | `hudsonia` | *Hudsonia montana* stage-projection matrices, 1985–1988 | `popbio` [@R-popbio] | real | | Das Gupta examples | worked examples from @dasgupta1993 | `DasGuptR` [@R-DasGuptR] | real (published) | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.table(object = c("leather", "icio_synth[['2010']]", "dk_mortality"), dimensions = c(paste(dim(leather$inter), collapse = " x "), paste(dim(icio_synth[["2010"]]$inter), collapse = " x "), paste(dim(dk_mortality), collapse = " x "))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|object |dimensions | |:--------------------|:----------| |leather |9 x 9 | |icio_synth[['2010']] |6 x 6 | |dk_mortality |192 x 5 |
::: ::: Real OECD/ADB ICIO tables are not bundled: they run to hundreds of megabytes and have restrictive licences. `load_icio()` and `load_icio_csv()` accept them directly. ## Reproducing this report ```sh Rscript -e 'renv::restore()' quarto render ``` All data are bundled or cached under `data-raw/cache/`, so rendering makes no network calls.
